definition: A promise by one party to cover the other party's losses, damages, or legal costs arising from specific events, such as a breach of contract or a third-party claim.
A clause that excuses a party from performing its obligations when extraordinary events beyond its control — like natural disasters, war, or government action — make performance impossible.
A private process for resolving disputes outside of court, where a neutral third party (the arbitrator) hears both sides and makes a binding decision.
An obligation to keep certain information secret and not share it with people outside the agreement, except as allowed by the contract.
The right to end a contract early because the other party broke one of its promises or violated a term of the agreement.
The right to end a contract early for any reason, or no reason at all, typically after giving advance notice.
A promise not to work for a competing business or start a competing business for a certain period of time and within a certain area.
A contract in which the parties agree not to share confidential information they learn from each other.
The date on which a contract's terms officially begin to apply.
A clause allowing a contract to be signed in multiple separate copies, each considered part of the same single agreement.
A clause stating that the written contract represents the complete agreement between the parties, replacing any earlier promises or discussions.
A formal change or addition to a contract after it has already been signed.
A formal way of informing the other party about something, usually required to be in writing and sent to a specific address.
The action or compensation a party can pursue when the other side breaks the contract, such as monetary damages or a court order.
Money awarded to compensate a party for loss or injury caused by the other party's breach of contract.
Legal responsibility for a loss, harm, or debt.
A clause that caps the amount of money one party can be forced to pay the other if something goes wrong, often excluding certain types of damages entirely.
Someone who is not a signer of the contract but who is still entitled to receive a benefit from it.
A clause stating that the contract's rights and obligations pass on to anyone who later takes over a party's business or role, such as a buyer or heir.
The process the parties agree to use for resolving disagreements, such as negotiation, mediation, arbitration, or litigation.
A process where a neutral third party helps the parties reach a voluntary agreement, without imposing a binding decision.
The legal time limit within which a party must file a lawsuit, after which the right to sue is lost.
A failure to take reasonable care, resulting in harm or damage to another person or their property.
A serious, reckless disregard for the safety or rights of others — more severe than ordinary carelessness.
An intentional act done knowing it is wrong or likely to cause harm, as opposed to an accident or mistake.
Something of value — money, services, or a promise — that each party gives in exchange for the other's promise, which is required to make a contract legally binding.
A significant failure to perform a contract's terms, serious enough that it undermines the whole purpose of the agreement and may allow the other party to terminate it.
A set amount of time given to a party to fix a breach or problem before the other party can take further action, such as terminating the contract.
Money, documents, or property held by a neutral third party until certain conditions of an agreement are met.
A legal claim against property that lets a creditor take or sell that property if a debt isn't paid.
Property or assets pledged as security for a loan or obligation, which can be taken if the obligation isn't fulfilled.
A failure to fulfill a legal or contractual obligation, such as missing a required payment or deadline.
A clause that allows a lender to demand full, immediate repayment of a loan if the borrower misses a payment or breaks another term.
The right of one party (often an insurer) who has paid a loss to step into the injured party's shoes and pursue the party actually responsible.
A legal document giving one person the authority to act on another person's behalf in financial, legal, or personal matters.
The replacement of one party in a contract with a new party, releasing the original party from its obligations, with everyone's agreement.
A legal principle that stops a person from going back on a promise or statement if someone else reasonably relied on it to their detriment.
An event caused entirely by nature — such as an earthquake, flood, or storm — that no one could have prevented or controlled.
A deal made between two parties who each act independently in their own interest, without one having special influence over the other.
Standard contract language that is used routinely across many agreements, often covering technical or procedural matters.
A clause specifying which state or country's laws will be used to interpret and enforce the contract.
The specific court or location where a legal dispute under the contract must be filed and heard.
A separate document, such as a schedule, form, or list, attached to a contract and referenced as part of the agreement.
Additional material added to a contract after it was originally written, to add new terms or clarify existing ones.
The introductory background section of a contract (often starting with 'Whereas') that explains why the parties are entering into the agreement.
Traditional closing language in a contract that introduces the signature section, confirming the parties intend to be bound by the agreement.
The voluntary giving up of a right, claim, or requirement under a contract.
A clause stating that if one part of the contract is found invalid or unenforceable, the rest of the contract still remains in effect.
The transfer of a party's rights or obligations under a contract to another person or entity.
A factual statement made by one party to induce the other party to enter the contract, which if false may lead to legal claims.
A promise that certain facts are true or that something will meet a certain standard, which can be legally enforced if broken.
A failure by one party to do what they promised to do under the terms of the agreement.
The specific set of laws (usually of a state or country) that will be used to interpret and enforce a contract.
The authority of a particular court to hear and decide a legal case.
A wrongful act, other than a breach of contract, that causes harm to someone and can lead to legal liability.
The minimum number of members who must be present at a meeting for decisions made there to be considered valid.
A legal obligation to act in the best interests of another person or party, putting their interests ahead of your own.
The formal approval of an action or agreement that makes it officially valid and binding.
A specific amount of money the parties agree in advance will be paid if one side breaches the contract, instead of calculating actual losses later.
